chapter: Los Angeles in 1935: school, jam sessions and the hobo trip west
title: Dust storm outside Amarillo
summary: Put off a freight train, he and other hoboes walked through a dust storm.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, we spent a little bit better than 24 hours trying to get out of Amarillo. Like, they had dust storms during that year, '35, which killed all the crops, you know. It was very bad; bad scene. We got on a train in Amarillo, freight, during that time you didn't have to get underneath the train. You could get on the train when it was standing still, you know, get inside the boxcars or, if it was moving, you'd have to get on the flat -- run and jump and catch it, get on the flatcars, you know.

But we'd get inside the boxcars and sometimes we would get between the cars, you know, which -- they called that the -- I forget the part of the train they'd call that. Anyway, we got about -- oh, I guess about 18 miles out of Amarillo, and they stopped the train for a shakedown. And they started at the first boxcar, and the train would move up an inch, and they'd get the others out of the next boxcar, and the next boxcar, until they got all the hobos off the train, at the end, the caboose. And the train went on out into the distance, and left us all out here in this vast space. Well, I guess it was about 20 of us.
And about five minutes after that train left, here comes a dust storm. Boy, you talk about awful. We're not here to talk about dust storms. We're here to talk about music.
It's part of (inaudible) your whole experience, though. I remember the dust storms, from Oklahoma.

Well, we joined hands and started to walk. We couldn't sit down, we'd get covered up, you know. And I was dressed for traveling. I had on about three pair of trousers, about three shirts, a sweater, and a hunter's leather jacket. It was reversible. Three-quarter length, it was leather on one side and courderoy on the other. And you know these tassle caps, that you can pull down over your ears? I had that. And when that storm come, I wanted to pull that cap off, but the only thing I could do was pull it down over my ears, over my face, you know, in order to keep the skin from getting beat off. But that didn't help any. My skin still got beat off my face. My eyelids had scabs on it, my face -- How'd you breathe?
The best we could. Now, the crew dwindled down to a precious few. (laughs)

Wait a minute, we weren't too far from a junction. I'll never forget it. Woodlawn Junction. But we went through some changes before we got to the junction. We were crossing the highways and cars just had on their headlights, just blowing their horns. That's the only way we kept from getting hit. We crossed the highway and we come on this farmhouse and the other part of the door was a glass pane, and you

could see in the house, and here's three fellows sitting there with their feet propped up one of these pot-bellied stoves, you know. We knocked on the door, Mexicans, whites, blacks, all looked the same because of this dust.

They turned around and looked at the window, and turned right back around the looked at the stove and started spitting on the stove. We said, 'Well, wow, that's cold,' so we walked about a mile further. We don't know what direction we were going. And we walked in, people turned their hounds loose on us, and we were falling over barbed wire fences. Everybody got lost. (laughs)
So -- all I could do was get away from that barbed wire fence, and just stand. Until finally, it let up. And everybody was just standing like I was, like posts; everyone was afraid to move, you know?

So I finally found my partner, my road buddy, and we walked on to Woodlawn Junction. And we see this fellow in a T-model Ford, a two-seater. And he was a preacher. And he was driving into Amarillo to sell some eggs. And we asked him and say, 'How much -- could we get a ride to Amarillo? How much will you charge us?' He said, 'How much money have you got?' We said, 'Fifty cents.' He said, 'Get in.'
